newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil starts deciding fate of Indian reserves.
newsitem.headline: Brazil starts deciding fate of Indian reserves.

text.p: Brazil on Thursday began deciding the fate of a disputed Amazon Indian reserve, a case pressure groups feared could set a "terrible" precedent for 199 other indigenous lands in Latin America's largest country.

Justice Minister Nelson Jobim, in Raposa/Serra do Sol in Roraima state to decide how to demarcate the territory, was likely to bend to pressure from local authorities and ranchers to reduce the land Indians consider theirs, officials said.

"The aim itself is not to reduce their land," said Byron Prestes Costa, an aide to the minister. "But we will have to find a compromise between the wishes of settlers, Indians and the state government."

Pressure groups and the National Indian Foundation (Funai) said Raposa could determine the destiny of up to 199 other Indian lands, which can now be contested in the courts under a law passed early this year.

Since Decree 1775 came into effect, 83 legal challenges have been filed and Funai said another 199 of Brazil's 556 Indian reserves remained vulnerable to legal claims, comprising almost half the 206 million acres (83.5 million hectares) recognised as indigenous land in Brazil.

Jobim was to meet church leaders and Indians seeking to have the entire Raposa area on the rainforest frontier with Guyana demarcated. He will also hear the views of state officials and local cattle ranchers who want the area reduced.
His most likely course of action has outraged pressure groups, who see it as a possible precedent for other cases.

"Everything indicates (he) is looking for a pretext to take a political decision. Once again Indian lands are being used as a bargaining chip for backroom political deals," said Stephan Schwartzman of U.S.-based Environmental Defence Fund.

Schwartzman said reducing the area, where armed ranchers frequently clash with Indians carrying bows and arrows, would be "tantamount to looking for bloodshed" and would seriously damage the Indians' constitutional land rights. The consequences would be "terrible," he added.

Funai has proposed demarcating all the area traditionally regarded as belonging to the 11,000 Indians of the Makuxi, Ingariko, Wapixana, Taurepang and Patamona tribes in Raposa. But after heated protests from the state government, officials in small towns that encroach on Indian land and farmers who hold land deeds in the area, the Justice Ministry put forward a counter-propsal, reducing the reserve.

Funai's director of land policy, Aureo Araujo Faleiros, told Reuters the Justice Ministry plan would place nearly 600 Indians in nine villages outside the protected area. It would still involve expelling some 240 farmers with legitimate claims at a cost of $6 million in compensation.

The Justice Ministry's Costa noted that almost 50 percent of Roraima had been declared Indian land, protected from outside interference, and said the state's opposition to demarcating a larger area in Raposa was to some extent understandable. "We have to treat their point of view, their desire for development, with kindness," Costa said.
